items.scenario: A 30-year-old woman takes sertraline 50 mg by mouth daily for anxiety and lorazepam 0.5 mg by mouth at bedtime as needed. She started ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth three times daily for knee pain. She has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding.
items.question: Which paired regimen poses the greatest risk?
options: Sertraline 50 mg daily with lorazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime as needed
Sertraline 50 mg daily with ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily
Lorazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime with cetirizine 10 mg daily
Sertraline 50 mg daily with a combined oral contraceptive

items.scenario: A 40-year-old woman has heartburn at least 3 days a week for 2 months. She had taken OTC ranitidine until products containing it were removed from the market. She has no trouble swallowing, bleeding, weight loss, or vomiting, and she is not pregnant.
items.question: Which recommendation is most appropriate now?
options: Omeprazole 20 mg by mouth once daily before breakfast for 8 weeks
Famotidine 10 mg by mouth once daily as needed
Ask her to restart ranitidine 150 mg by mouth twice daily
Calcium carbonate 750 mg by mouth only after meals

items.scenario: A 30-year-old man takes phenytoin 300 mg by mouth daily, as 100 mg three times daily, for epilepsy. Seizures have increased. The total phenytoin level is 8 mcg/mL and albumin is 4.2 g/dL. He started omeprazole 20 mg daily for GERD one week ago.
items.question: Which action best addresses the increased seizures?
options: Increase phenytoin to 330 mg daily and recheck the level in 7 days
Switch omeprazole to famotidine 20 mg twice daily and keep phenytoin at 300 mg daily
Add levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily and keep phenytoin at 300 mg daily
Stop omeprazole and keep phenytoin at 300 mg daily

items.scenario: A 55-year-old man with COPD uses tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily and albuterol 90 mcg, 2 inhalations every 4 to 6 hours as needed. He has had 2 exacerbations this year, neither requiring hospitalization. The blood eosinophil count is 80 cells/µL. He is not asthmatic.
items.question: Which change best reduces further exacerbations?
options: Add theophylline 300 mg by mouth daily
Add montelukast 10 mg by mouth daily
Switch to tiotropium/olodaterol 2.5/2.5 mcg, 2 inhalations once daily
Add fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 mcg, 1 inhalation twice daily

items.scenario: A 62-year-old man with COPD uses tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily and albuterol as needed. Dyspnea is worse and he uses the rescue inhaler daily. FEV1 is 55% predicted. He has had no exacerbation in the past year. The blood eosinophil count is 90 cells/µL.
items.question: Which inhaler should replace tiotropium monotherapy?
options: Budesonide/formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, 2 inhalations twice daily
Umeclidinium/vilanterol 62.5/25 mcg, 1 inhalation once daily
Montelukast 10 mg by mouth daily, with tiotropium continued
Ipratropium 17 mcg, 2 inhalations four times daily

items.scenario: S.G. is a 34-year-old woman who had a traumatic splenectomy 14 days ago. Records show no adult Tdap and no pneumococcal, meningococcal, or Hib vaccine. She is not pregnant. Influenza vaccine is in season.
items.question: Which vaccines should the pharmacist give today? Select all that apply.
options: Tdap 0.5 mL IM once, plus Hib 0.5 mL IM once
Inactivated influenza vaccine 0.5 mL IM once this season
PCV20 0.5 mL IM once, with no PPSV23 after it
Recombinant zoster vaccine 0.5 mL IM now and again in 2 to 6 months because of asplenia
MenACWY 0.5 mL IM now and again in 8 weeks, then a booster every 5 years, plus a MenB series

items.scenario: A 30-year-old woman with asthma requests her seasonal influenza vaccine. She uses albuterol 90 mcg, 2 inhalations as needed. Eating eggs has caused hives only, never anaphylaxis, wheezing, or a hospital visit.
items.question: Which plan is appropriate?
options: Give any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL IM, and observe 15 minutes as for any vaccine
Give the vaccine but pretreat with diphenhydramine 50 mg
Use only an egg-free vaccine and observe her for 30 minutes
Defer vaccination until she is evaluated by an allergist

items.scenario: A 30-year-old woman with no chronic illnesses asks for an influenza vaccine. She says she is allergic to eggs. She is taking no medicines. Her immunization history is otherwise up to date.
items.question: Which counseling point is correct?
options: She can receive any age-appropriate influenza vaccine, 0.5 mL IM, with the usual 15-minute observation
She needs an egg-free product and a 30-minute observation
Give half a dose, 0.25 mL IM, because of the egg allergy
Egg allergy means she should skip influenza vaccine this season

items.scenario: A 42-year-old man refills lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. For the past week he has had a persistent dry cough that started after lisinopril. Blood pressure today is 130/85 mm Hg. He has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which finding needs action before the refill is treated as routine?
options: No known drug allergies
Persistent dry cough after starting lisinopril
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg
Request to refill atorvastatin

items.scenario: A 30-year-old man takes lisinopril 20 mg by mouth daily for hypertension. He feels well. Potassium is 5.8 mEq/L, creatinine is stable, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. He has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which result should change therapy today?
options: No known drug allergies
Potassium of 5.8 mEq/L
Lisinopril dose of 20 mg daily by itself
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg

items.scenario: A 50-year-old man refills lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. He feels well except for a persistent dry cough. Blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg and LDL cholesterol is 90 mg/dL.
items.question: Which finding should the pharmacist address before calling the visit routine?
options: LDL cholesterol of 90 mg/dL
No medicine change of any kind
Persistent dry cough
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg

items.scenario: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidemia takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. She feels dizzy when she stands up quickly. Seated blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Lipids are at goal and she has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which finding needs evaluation before she leaves?
options: No known drug allergies
Seated blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg
Use of atorvastatin 20 mg daily
Dizziness when standing up quickly

items.scenario: A 45-year-old woman is starting lisinopril 20 mg by mouth daily for hypertension. She reports a persistent dry cough, blood pressure 130/85 mm Hg, a father with hypertension, and a body mass index of 27 kg/m². She takes no other medicines and has no known drug allergies.
items.question: Which finding should change the plan today?
options: Persistent dry cough
Blood pressure of 130/85 mm Hg
Body mass index of 27 kg/m²
Family history of hypertension

items.scenario: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and CKD has an eGFR of 48 mL/min/1.73 m². He takes amlodipine 10 mg daily and lisinopril 20 mg daily. Blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg and both ankles are swollen. Potassium is 4.4 mEq/L and creatinine is stable.
items.question: Which adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg by mouth once daily
Raise lisinopril to 80 mg daily
Stop lisinopril because he has CKD
Raise amlodipine to 15 mg daily

items.scenario: A 30-year-old client with type 1 diabetes is treated for diabetic ketoacidosis with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. After 6 hours, glucose is 240 mg/dL, pH is 7.26, anion gap is 18 mEq/L, and potassium is 4.1 mEq/L. The client is nauseated and not eating.
items.question: Which prescription should the nurse anticipate?
options: Add dextrose to the IV fluid and continue the insulin infusion
Switch to subcutaneous insulin and start a regular diet
Increase the insulin infusion to 0.2 units/kg/hour without dextrose
Stop the insulin infusion because glucose is below 250 mg/dL
